{{nihongo|'''Hiraoka Shrine'''|枚岡神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Kawachi Province]].

=== Overview ===
{{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine (Heibonsha)|1986}} is located at the western foot of {{ill|Ikoma Mountains|Q11574917|qid=Q11574917}} in eastern Osaka Prefecture, facing west. It is said to have originated from {{ill|Mountain worship|Q93697439|qid=Q93697439}} at Kozudake on the back mountain, and is known as the {{ill|Ujigami|Q767655|qid=Q767655}} of the Nakatomi clan, whose main deity is {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|Q2564508|qid=Q2564508|lt=Amagoyane no Mikoto}}, the ancestor of {{ill|Nakatomi clan|Q1198447|qid=Q1198447}}.

The {{ill|Fujiwara clan|Q641628|qid=Q641628}}, which separated from the Nakatomi clan, established {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|Q714559|qid=Q714559}} as the {{ill|Ujigami|Q767655|qid=Q767655}}. When it was first built, two of the four deities enshrined were the spirits of our company's Amagoyane-no-Mikoto and Hime-kami, which is why it is also called ``Moto Kasuga.'' After that, as the Fujiwara clan prospered, its reverence increased, and in the {{ill|Heian period|Q193292|qid=Q193292}}, {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|Q11591025|qid=Q11591025}} reached the highest rank of Shoichii, Order 3rd Class. After {{ill|Middle Ages|Q12554|qid=Q12554}}, it was revered as {{ill|Ichinomiya|Q1656379|qid=Q1656379}} of {{ill|Kawachi Province|Q1047150|qid=Q1047150}}, and {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Meiji Restoration}}, it is one of the most important ancient shrines in the country and is ranked as the highest {{ill|Q712534|lt=Kanpei Taisha}} in the {{ill|Q712534|lt=Modern Shrine Ranking System}}.The main shrine is in the {{ill|Kasuga-zukuri|Q3193781|qid=Q3193781|lt=Kasuga}} quadruple-Hiraoka-zukuri style, and is designated as a {{ill|Tangible Cultural Property (Japan)|Q2901860|qid=Q2901860}} by Higashiosaka City. In addition, many rituals have been passed down to the present day, and among the special rituals, the porridge fortune-telling ritual is an intangible folk cultural property that should be recorded in Osaka Prefecture.|Q11642584|selection It has been selected as an intangible folk cultural property}}, and the Shimenawake Shinto ritual has been designated as an {{ill|Folk Cultural Property|Q24895900|qid=Q24895900|lt=intangible folk cultural property}} by Higashiosaka City.

=== Company name ===
Regarding the company name of Hiraoka Shrine, the following main names can be found in historical sources:
* Amagoyane no Mikoto - “{{ill|Shoku Nihon Kōki|cs|Šoku Nihonkóki|de|Shoku Nihon Kōki|es|Shoku Nihon Kōki|ff|Shoku Nihon Kōki|fr|Shoku nihon kōki|ja|続日本後紀|ko|속일본후기|pt|Shoku Nihon Kōki|zh|續日本後紀|qid=Q1041301}}”<ref group="Hara" name="Jowa 3rd year article"/><ref group="Hara" name="Jowa 6th year article"/>
* Hiraoka Grand Shrine - “Shoku Nihon Koki” <ref group="Hara" name="Jowa 10th year article"/>
* Hiraoka Kami - "{{ill|Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku|Q1052905|qid=Q1052905}}" <ref group="Hara" name="Narihira 3-year article"/>・"{{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|Q1052981|qid=Q1052981}}" <ref group="Hara" name="Article dated October 7th year of Jogan">Article dated October 21, 865, "Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku" (Refer to {{Harvnb|Collection of Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials}}). </ref><ref group="Hara" name="Article dated December 7th year of Jogan">Article dated December 17, 865, "Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku" (see {{Harvnb|Collection of Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials}}). </ref>・“{{ill|Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448}}” Shijisaijou<ref group="Hara" name="Shikisaijou"/>
* Hiraoka Tenjiyane no Mikoto - “Nihon Sandai Jiroki” <ref group="Hara" name="Jogan 1st Year New Year Article"/>* Hiraokajin - "{{ill|Shinshō Kyakuchokufushō|ja|新抄格勅符抄|qid=Q11502312}}" <ref group="Hara" name="Shinsho Kakuchofusho"/>・"Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku" <ref group="Hara" name="Article dated September 1st year of Jogan">Article dated September 8, 1st year of Jogan (859) from "Nihon Sandai Jironroku" (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}). </ref>
* Hiraoka Shrine - "Engishiki" {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|abstract|Q11064932|fr|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|ja|延喜式神名帳|simple|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|zh|延喜式神名帳|qid=Q11064932|lt=Shinmyocho}}<ref name="Shinmyocho" group="Hara"/>・Temporary festival<ref group="Hara" name="Meishin Festival"/>
* Hiraokasha - "Engishiki" {{ill|Temporary Festival|Q11612499|qid=Q11612499}}<ref group="Hara" name="Prayer God Festival"/>・Shiji Festival 2<ref group="Hara" name="Shiji Festival 2"/>
As seen above, since {{ill|Ancient history|Q41493|qid=Q41493}}, the characters ``Hiraoka'' and ``Hiraoka'' have been used together in the company name.{{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine (Heibonsha)|1986}}{{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine (Gods)|2000}} This trend was followed until {{ill|Early modern period|an|Edat Moderna|ar|الحقبة الحديثة المبكرة|ast|Edá Moderna|az|Erkən modern dövr|bar|Friae Neizeid|be|Ранні Новы час|bn|প্রারম্ভিক আধুনিক যুগ|br|Amzerioù modern|ca|Edat moderna|cs|Raný novověk|cy|Cyfnod Modern Cynnar|da|Tidlig moderne tid|de|Frühe Neuzeit|el|Πρώιμη νεότερη περίοδος|eo|Frua moderna epoko|es|Edad Moderna|et|Varauusaeg|eu|Aro Modernoa|fa|دوران نوین آغازین|fi|Varhaismoderni|fr|Époque moderne|gl|Idade Moderna|gn|Ára Ko'ãgagua|he|העת החדשה המוקדמת|hi|प्रारंभिक आधुनिक काल|hu|Korai újkor|ia|Etate Moderne|id|Periode modern awal|io|Modern-epoko|it|Età moderna|ja|近世|kbp|Alɩwaatʊ kɩfatʊ (Période moderne)|ko|근세|ku|Destpêka Dema Nûjen|kw|Oos Arnowydh A-Varr|lb|Neizäit|lfn|Eda moderna|li|Vreugmodernen Tied|lij|Etæ Modèrna|lld|Storia moderna|lmo|Età Modèrna|lo|ຍຸກ​ສະ​ໄຫມ​ຕົ້ນ​|lt|Naujieji amžiai|lv|Agrīnie jaunie laiki|mg|Andro Vaovao|mk|Ран нов век|new|प्रारम्भिक आधुनिक काल|nl|Vroegmoderne tijd|nn|Tidleg nytid|no|Tidlig moderne tid|oc|Edat Modèrna|pap|Edad Moderno|pcd|Histoère modérne|pl|Nowożytność|ps|لومړۍ معاصره دوره|pt|Idade Moderna|rm|Temp modern tempriv|ro|Epoca modernă timpurie|ru|Раннее Новое время|sc|Edade moderna|sh|Rani novi vijek|simple|Early modern period|sq|Periudha e hershme moderne|sr|Rani novi vek|stq|Eermodärne Tied|sv|Tidigmoderna tiden|th|สมัยใหม่ตอนต้น|tl|Makabagong kasaysayan|tr|Yeni Çağ|tt|Иртә яңа заман|uk|Ранній новий період|vi|Thời kỳ cận đại|vls|Nieuwn tyd|wuu|近世|yi|נייע צייט|zh|近世|zh_yue|近代史|qid=Q5308718}}, and the word ``Hiraoka'' is also recognized on the stone monuments and {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=lanterns}} that remain today {{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine (Gods)|2000}}.

=== Enshrined God ===
The following four deities are currently enshrined. </ref><ref name="History">[http://www.hiraoka-jinja.org/history/index.html History] (Hiraoka Shrine homepage). </ref>. One pillar is enshrined in each of the four main halls (first, second, third, and fourth halls).
:* First Hall: {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|Q2564508|qid=Q2564508|lt=Amagoyane no Mikoto}} (Amenokoyane no Mikoto) - The main deity, the ancestral deity of the Nakatomi clan.
:* Second Hall: {{ill|Himegami|Q22070227|qid=Q22070227|lt=Hime-gokami}} (Hime-mikami) - Amagoyane Mikoto.
:* Third Hall: {{ill|Futsunushi|Q1107286|qid=Q1107286|lt=Tunetsu no Mikoto}} (Futsunushi no Mikoto, Saishu no Mikoto) - {{ill|Katori Jingū|Q372380|qid=Q372380}} Enshrined deity.
:* Fourth Hall: {{ill|Takemikazuchi|lt=Takemikazuchi|Q1502690|qid=Q1502690|qid=Q1502690|lt=Takemikazuchi no Mikoto}} (Takemikazuchi no Mikoto, Takemikazuchi no Mikoto) - {{ill|Kashima Jingū|Q706499|qid=Q706499}}Enshrined deity.There are currently four deities enshrined, but "{{ill|Shoku Nihon Kōki|cs|Šoku Nihonkóki|de|Shoku Nihon Kōki|es|Shoku Nihon Kōki|ff|Shoku Nihon Kōki|fr|Shoku nihon kōki|ja|続日本後紀|ko|속일본후기|pt|Shoku Nihon Kōki|zh|續日本後紀|qid=Q1041301}}" {{ill|Jōwa (Heian period)|Q1075605|qid=Q1075605|lt=Jowa}}3 ({{ill|836|Q24957|qid=Q24957}}) Article <ref group="Hara" Name="Jowa 3rd Year Article"/> was the first time I saw it, and in ancient times only the two pillars of Amagoyane-no-Mikoto and Hime-jin were recognized. The first mention of the four deities enshrined in the literature is in "{{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|Q1052981|qid=Q1052981}}" {{ill|Jōgan|Q1075635|qid=Q1075635|lt=Jōkan}} 7th year ({{ill|865|Q30350|qid=Q30350}}) <ref group="Hara" Name="December 7th year of Jogan"/> "Hiraoka Shrine Shizen" is written {{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine (Heibonsha)|1986}}. {{ill|Enchō|Q1327274|qid=Q1327274|lt=Extension}} "{{ill|Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448}}" established in 5 years ({{ill|927|ab|927|af|927|am|927 እ.ኤ.አ.|an|927|ar|927|ary|927|ast|927|avk|927|az|927|azb|۹۲۷ (میلادی)|bar|927|bcl|927|be|927|be_x_old|927|bg|927|bn|৯২৭|bpy|মারি ৯২৭|br|927|bs|927.|ca|927|cdo|927 nièng|ceb|927|ckb|٩٢٧|crh|927|cs|927|csb|927|cv|927|cy|927|da|927|de|927|el|927|eml|927|eo|927|es|927|et|927|eu|927|fa|۹۲۷ (میلادی)|fi|927|fo|927|fr|927|fy|927|ga|927|gan|927年|gd|927|gl|927|he|927|hi|927|hr|927.|ht|927 (almanak jilyen)|hu|927|hy|927|id|927|ilo|927|io|927|is|927|it|927|ja|927年|jv|927|ka|927|kaa|927|kk|927 жыл|ko|927년|la|927|lb|927|lij|927|lmo|927|lt|927 m.|lv|927. gads|map_bms|927|mdf|927|mg|927|mhr|927|mi|927|mk|927|mr|इ.स. ९२७|mrj|927 и|ms|927|mzn|۹۲۷|nah|927|nap|927|nds|927|new|सन् ९२७|nl|927|nn|927|no|927|nrm|927|nso|927|oc|927|or|୯୨୭|os|927-æм аз|pl|927|pnb|927|pt|927|qu|927|ro|927|ru|927 год|rue|927|sa|९२७|scn|927|sd|927ع|se|927|sh|927.|shn|927|si|927|sk|927|smn|927|sq|927|sr|927|su|927|sv|927|sw|927|tg|Соли 927|th|พ.ศ. 1470|tk|927|tl|927|tly|927|tr|927|tt|927 ел|uk|927|ur|927ء|uz|927|vec|927|vi|927|war|927|wuu|927年|xmf|927|zh|927年|zh_min_nan|927 nî|zh_yue|927年|qid=Q30470}}) The enshrined deity in group="Hara"/> is listed as 4 deities {{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine 4 deities (Shikinaisha)|1979}} The {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Honjibutsu}} of the main deity Amagoyane no Mikoto is {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|Q604687|qid=Q604687}}{{Sfn|Ichinomiya system in medieval countries|2000|pp=48-49}}.

=== About the enshrined deity ===
[[File:Kasuga-taisha11bs3200.jpg|thumb|220px|right|{{Center|{{ill|Kasuga-taisha|Q714559|qid=Q714559}} ({{ill|Nara Prefecture|Q131287|qid=Q131287}}{{ill|Nara (city)|Q169134|qid=Q169134}})}}{{Small|Fujiwara clan shrine. At the time of its construction, the spirits of Amagoyane-no-Mikoto and Hime-kami were solicited from Hiraoka Shrine, and they are enshrined in the third and fourth halls, respectively. }}]]The main enshrined deity, {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|Q2564508|qid=Q2564508|lt='''Amenokoyane-no-Mikoto'' (Amenokoyane)}}, is known as the ancestral deity of the ancient clan ``''{{ill|Nakatomi clan|Q1198447|qid=Q1198447}}'' (Nakatomiuji, Nakatomi-ren) and the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|Q641628|qid=Q641628}}, which was separated from the Nakatomi clan. In "{{ill|Kojiki|Q813031|qid=Q813031}}" and "{{ill|Nihon Shoki|Q813935|qid=Q813935}}," this god appears to be Nakatomi no kami, Nakatomi ren toso, and Nakatomi kamiso. When {{ill|Amaterasu|Q455602|qid=Q455602}}'s {{ill|Amano-Iwato|Q3231835|qid=Q3231835|lt=Iwatogakure}} It is said that he performed religious rituals with Tama no Mikoto}} ({{ill|Inbe clan|fa|خاندان اینبه|ja|忌部氏|pl|Inbe (ród)|simple|Inbe clan|th|ตระกูลอิมเบะ|zh|忌部氏|qid=Q8189229}} ancestor deity), It is recorded that he followed the god as one of the five gods (Goban-o) at the time of the descent of the descendants of the Tenson (Mikoto) {{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine (Heibonsha)|1986}}. In "{{ill|Shinsen Shōjiroku|de|Shinsen Shōjiroku|fr|Shinsen shōjiroku|ja|新撰姓氏録|ko|신찬성씨록|ru|Синсэн сёдзироку|zh|新撰姓氏錄|qid=Q1045362}}", there are many Nakatomi clans in Kawachi Province, and among them, the Hiraoka clan (Hiraokaren) is said to be our Hosai clan.{{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine (Heibonsha)|1986}}{{Sfn|Hikaru Matsuo|2014}}.{{ill|Himegami|Q22070227|qid=Q22070227}}, along with Amagoyane no Mikoto, is the consort deity of Amagoyane no Mikoto. </ref>. The first written reference to the deity being enshrined is in the 3rd year of the Jowa era (836). The specific name of the god is not known in literature, but according to the shrine's legend it is Amemizutamateruhime no mikoto.<ref name="Yoshio"/> It should also be noted that in literature, Amagoyane-no-Mikoto and Hime-kami are always described as a pair {{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine (Gods)|2000}}. ``Engishiki'' ``Kasuga Festival Oratory'' <ref group="Hara"> ``Engishiki'' Volume 8 (Norito) Kasuga Festival Article. </ref>, when the Fujiwara clan founded {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|Q714559|qid=Q714559}} ({{ill|Nara Prefecture|Q131287|qid=Q131287}}{{ill|Nara (city)|Q169134|qid=Q169134}}) as a guardian deity, It is said that he enshrined the spirits of Hiraoka Zatennoko Yakone no Mikoto (Amagoyane no Mikoto) and Hime deity {{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine (Heibonsha)|1986}}{{Sfn|Matsuo Hikaru|2014}}, and even now, both deities are enshrined in the third and fourth halls of Kasuga Taisha Shrine.The other two enshrined deities, {{ill|Futsunushi|Q1107286|qid=Q1107286|lt=Futunushi}} and {{ill|Takemikazuchi|lt=Takemikazuchi|Q1502690|qid=Q1502690|qid=Q1502690|lt=Takemikazuchi}}, are respectively {{ill|Katori Jingū|Q372380|qid=Q372380}} ({{jalink|Chiba Prefecture|Q {{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine (Heibonsha)|1986}} is the main enshrined deity of 80011}}{{ill|Katori, Chiba|Q858357|qid=Q858357}}) and {{ill|Kashima Jingū|Q706499|qid=Q706499}} ({{ill|Ibaraki Prefecture|Q83273|qid=Q83273}}{{ill|Kashima, Ibaraki|Q467471|qid=Q467471}}). The first written mention of the deity enshrined in our company is the aforementioned Jogan 7th year (865) article <ref group="hara" name="December 7th year of Jogan article"/>. Both deities, like Amagoyane-no-Mikoto and Hime-kami, were offered at the time of the founding of Kasuga Taisha Shrine (Kasuga Taisha Shrine Second Hall and First Hall) {{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine (Heibonsha)|1986}}{{Sfn|Hikaru Matsuo|2014}}, At Hiraoka Shrine, as with Kasuga Taisha, both deities are enshrined, and from 2 to 4 deities are enshrined. It is said that it was changed to {{ill|Jingo-keiun|Q1373049|qid=Q1373049}}2 ({{ill|768|Q29961|qid=Q29961}}), which is said to be the founding year of Kasuga Taisha Shrine.<ref group="Note">The exact year in which Kasugasha was founded is not clear. ``Jingo Keiun 2nd Year'' is based on the shrine diary of Kasuga Taisha Shrine, and is supported by the article dated August 26, 1980 in the ``Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku'' (``Kasuga Taisha Shrine'', ``National History Dictionary'', Yoshikawa Kobunkan). {{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine (Heibonsha)|1986}}{{Sfn|Ichinomiya system in medieval countries|2000|pp=48-49}}{{Sfn|Hikaru Matsuo|2014}} (in the shrine biography) jalink|Houki|Q18520676}}9 ({{ill|778|Q30452|qid=Q30452}}). In addition, "Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku" <ref group="Hara"> "Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku" article dated July 10, 860. There is also a theory that the shrines of Mikafuto no Mikoto and Hikosa Jifutō no Mikoto in Kawachi Province are compared to Takemikatsuchi no Mikoto and Tsunetsu Nushi no Mikoto of our company. In addition to the theory that it is compared to the two shrines of Hiraoka Shrine, there is another theory that it is compared to {{ill|Yuge Shrine|Q11487076|qid=Q11487076|lt=Yuge Shrine}} in Wakae District, Kawachi Province. </ref>.

=== History ===

=== Founding ===
In the shrine biography ("Genyoki" etc.), three years before the enthronement of {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|ar|الإمبراطور جينمو|arz|الامبراطور جينمو|as|জিম্মু|az|Cimmu|bcl|Emperador Jimmu|be|Імператар Дзіму|ca|Jinmu|cdo|Sìng-ū Tiĕng-huòng|ckb|ئیمپراتۆر جینمو|cs|Džimmu|de|Jimmu|el|Αυτοκράτορας Τζίμου|eo|Imperiestro Jinmu|es|Jinmu Tennō|et|Jimmu|eu|Jimmu enperadorea|fa|امپراتور جینمو|fi|Jinmu|fr|Jinmu|hak|Sṳ̀n-vú Thiên-fòng|he|ג'ימו, קיסר יפן|hi|सम्राट जिममु|hr|Jinmu|hu|Dzsinmu japán császár|id|Jimmu|it|Jinmu|ja|神武天皇|jv|Jimmu Tenno|ka|ძიმუ|ko|진무 천황|kw|Emperour Jimmu|la|Jimmu|lt|Imperatorius Džinmu|lv|Džimmu|mn|Эзэн Хаан Жиммү|mr|जिम्मू|ms|Maharaja Jimmu|my|ဂျင်းမူ ဧကရာဇ်|nl|Jimmu|no|Jimmu|pl|Jimmu|pt|Jimmu|ru|Император Дзимму|sh|Car Jimmu|simple|Emperor Jimmu|sl|Cesar Džinmu|sr|Џинму|sv|Jimmu|th|จักรพรรดิจิมมุ|tl|Emperador Jimmu|tr|Jimmu|uk|Імператор Дзімму|uz|Jimmu|vi|Thiên hoàng Jimmu|war|Emperador Jimmu|wuu|神武天皇|zh|神武天皇|zh_classical|神武天皇|zh_min_nan|Sîn-bú Thian-hông|zh_yue|神武天皇|qid=Q200188}}, on the occasion of {{ill|Jimmu's Eastern Expedition|fa|اردوکشی شرقی جینمو|fr|Expédition orientale de Jimmu|ja|神武東征|ko|진무 동정|zh|神武東征|qid=Q11590444}}, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Amatsune no Mikoto}} is said to have started with the enshrinement of the two gods Amagoyane-no-Mikoto and Hime-kami by imperial order to Kamitsudake on the eastern mountain.{{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine (Heibonsha)|1986}}{{Sfn|Matsuo Hikaru|2014}}<ref name="historical book"/>. Later, in the first year of {{ill|Hakuchi (era)|Q540118|qid=Q540118}} ({{ill|650|Q30179|qid=Q30179}}), the Hiraoka Ren (Hiraoka clan) and others moved it from Kozudake to its current location.The Amatsune no Mikoto that appears in the above legend is from the "{{ill|Nihon Shoki|Q813935|qid=Q813935}}" Pre-Enthronement Period of Emperor Jinmu <ref group="Hara"> "Nihon Shoki" Pre-Enthronement Period of Emperor Jimmu October Shintori (5th) article in the year of Kotora. In </ref>, he appears to have married Usazuhime, the founder of Tsukushi's Susa Kunizukuri, and is said to be a vassal of Emperor Jimmu and a distant ancestor of the Nakatomi clan. Although the historical reality of the founding tradition is not clear, historical research indicates that the shrine was founded by mountain worship at Kozudake {{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine (Heibonsha)|1986}}. The ritual was carried out by the Hiraoka clan, an ancient clan in the area.{{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine (Heibonsha)|1986}} There is a theory that because the Oka clan and the Nakatomi clan were related, the enshrined deity became Amagoyane no Mikoto, the ancestor of the Nakatomi clan.{{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine (Heibonsha)|1986}}{{Sfn|Hikaru Matsuo|2014}}.

In addition, among the place names that appear in "{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Japanese name extract}}", this place is compared to Toyoura-go in {{ill|Kawachi Province|Q1047150|qid=Q1047150}}{{ill|Kawachi District, Tochigi|Q44611|qid=Q44611}}, but {{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine Four Seats (Shikiuchi-sha) |1979 }}{{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine (Gods)|2000}}, In the neighboring district of Kawachi Province {{ill|Sasara district|Q11632569|qid=Q11632569}}, there is Hiraoka-go (variant version is Makioka-go), and there is a theory that this place is the origin of Hiraoka Shrine.{{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine (Gods)|2000}}.

==== Medieval/Early modern ====
From the end of the {{ill|Heian period|Q193292|qid=Q193292}}, it is said to have been revered as {{ill|Ichinomiya|Q1656379|qid=Q1656379}} of Kawachi Province {{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine (Heibonsha)|1986}}. However, as a historical document showing Ichinomiya status, there is a "annual tribute order for Jingikan shrines" in the first year of {{ill|Eiman|Q1193868|qid=Q1193868}} ({{ill|1165|Q19676|qid=Q19676}}), which includes our company, Onchi Shrine, and Yuge Shrine ({{ill|Yuge Shrine|Q11487076|qid=Q11487076|lt=Yuge Shrine}}), but there are no documents related to Hiraoka Shrine that specify Ichinomiya in the {{ill|Middle Ages|Q12554|qid=Q12554}} period. The description can only be seen in ``{{ill|Dai Nippon Koku Ichinomiya Ki|Q11435648|qid=Q11435648}}'' and ``Ruiju Zeikensho'' {{Sfn|Ichinomiya system in medieval countries|2000|pp=48-49}}.

In the first year of {{ill|Kenji (era)|Q1327993|qid=Q1327993}} ({{ill|1275|Q5529|qid=Q5529}}), (Nara City)|Q1203935|Eison|Q11410722}} of Saidaiji Temple led a pilgrimage of over 100 monks, and {{jalink|Mongol Invasion|Q208156|Mongol Invasion] {{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine (Heibonsha)|1986}}{{Sfn|Ichinomiya System in Medieval Countries|2000|pp=48-49}}, which is translating and praising the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Great Pannya Sutra}}.

=== Shinto priest ===
The priesthood of Hiraoka Shrine is said to have been held by the ``Hiraoka clan'' (Hiraoka clan) in {{ill|Ancient history|Q41493|qid=Q41493}}. The Hiraoka clan is one of the Nakatomi clans, and is listed in "{{ill|Shinsen Shōjiroku|de|Shinsen Shōjiroku|fr|Shinsen shōjiroku|ja|新撰姓氏録|ko|신찬성씨록|ru|Синсэн сёдзироку|zh|新撰姓氏錄|qid=Q1045362}}" <ref group="Hara">"Shinsen Sōjiroku" Kamibetsu Kawachi Province Hiraoka Renjo. </ref> says that he is a descendant of Taimi Omi, the 14th grandson of Tsuhaya Tamami no Mikoto. In the same record, many of the Nakatomi clans in Kawachi Province are considered to be the descendants of Tsuhayadama no Mikoto (the ancestor of Amagoyane no Mikoto), and their character is different from that of the main sect of the Nakatomi clan, which is the descendant of Amagoyane no Mikoto.{{Sfn|Hikaru Matsuo|2014}}.In national history, in the 10th year of the Jowa era (843) <ref group="Hara" name="Article 10 of the Jowa era"/>, it is said that the priests of Hiraoka Daijinja Shrine and others were entrusted with the scepter, and in the 7th year of the Jogan era (865) <ref group="Hara" In the name="October 7th year of Jogan article"/>, it appears that one ``Hiraoka Shinto Priest'' was provided with silk threads for the spring and winter colors, but it is assumed that the Hiraoka Ren was in charge of these Shinto Priests {{Sfn|Hiraoka (Ancient Clan Encyclopedia)|2015}}. In addition, the official organization is the ``Engishiki'' <ref group="Hara" In the name="Shijisaijou"/>, there are descriptions of Shinto priests, Monoki, Negi, Shuku, Dankin, flute makers, 2 Urabes, and 8 Zenbes, but {{Sfn|Ichinomiya system in medieval countries|2000|pp=48-49}}, "{{ill|Ruijufusenshō|Q11665188|qid=Q11665188}}" <ref group="hara">"Ruijufusensho" Daijokanfu dated May 11, 952. According to </ref> and others, the priest, Monoki, seems to have been appointed by {{ill|Ōnakatomi clan|Q11431853|qid=Q11431853}} (Hiraoka clan) {{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine (Heibonsha)|1986}}{{Sfn|Ichinomiya system in medieval countries|2000|pp=48-49}}. {{ill|Kangen|Q1194187|qid=Q1194187}}3 year ({{ill|1245|Q5440|qid=Q5440}}) document <ref group="Hara"> "Hiradoki" Heikei Takashomon dated New Year 29, Kangen 3 year (1245). According to </ref>, since the appointment of Kimeifu at the time of {{ill|Emperor Shirakawa|Q60949|qid=Q60949|lt=Shirakawain}}, people other than the Hiraoka clan have been appointed to the priesthood position, and even within the Hiraoka clan, the Tametomo style has continued. It is said that the Yoriyasu school divided into two groups and fought against each other.Since the Middle Ages, the '''{{ill|Mizuhashi clan|Q11549239|qid=Q11549239}}''' (Mizuhayashi) was the chief priest, and the Torii clan was the chief priest. The Mizuhashi clan is a clan with the Fujiwara surname that claims to be descendants of the Hiraoka clan, and grew from a priest to a feudal lord (territorial lord) in the medieval period by inheriting the positions of social affairs, head priest, and head priest.{{Sfn|Ichinomiya system in medieval countries|2000|pp=48-49}}. Although it declined during the {{ill|Sengoku period|Q204023|qid=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period}}, it continued as a Shinto priest at Hiraoka Shrine until the end of the Edo period {{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine (Heibonsha)|1986}}{{Sfn|Hikaru Matsuo|2014}}.

=== Shrine building construction ===
{{ill|Tengi|Q1193591|qid=Q1193591}}4 ({{ja link|1056 years|Q19375}})・{{ill|Kanji (era)|Q1193874|qid=Q1193874}}5 years ({{ill|1091|Q19468|qid=Q19468}})・{ {jalink|Hoji|Q1327400}} 1st year ({{ill|1247|Q5482|qid=Q5482}}), {{ill|Gentoku|Q1327385|qid=Q1327385}}2nd year It is said that in ({{ill|1330|Q5996|qid=Q5996}}), shrine buildings were burnt down and shrines were transferred.{{Sfn|Ichinomiya system in medieval countries|2000|pp=48-49}}. According to the same book, it was in decline during the Muromachi period, but was revived by shrine parishioners in {{ill|Bunmei|Q1193544|qid=Q1193544|lt=Bunmei}} ({{ill|1475|Q6608|qid=Q6608}}) {{Sfn|Ichinomiya system in medieval countries|2000|pp=48-49}}.In {{ill|Tenshō (Momoyama period)|Q1145058|qid=Q1145058}}7 ({{ill|1579|Q6709|qid=Q6709}}), {{jalink|Oda Nobunaga|Q171411} The main shrine and 17 shrines and subsidiary shrines were destroyed by fire during the 1979 war. After that, it was rebuilt by {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyori|be|Таётомі Хідэёры|ca|Toyotomi Hideyori|cs|Hidejori Tojotomi|de|Toyotomi Hideyori|el|Τογιοτόμι Χιντεγιόρι|eo|Toyotomi Hideyori|es|Toyotomi Hideyori|eu|Toyotomi Hideyori|fa|تویوتومی هیده‌یوری|fi|Toyotomi Hideyori|fr|Toyotomi Hideyori|id|Toyotomi Hideyori|it|Toyotomi Hideyori|ja|豊臣秀頼|ko|도요토미 히데요리|la|Fideyorus|lt|Tojotomi Hidejori|ms|Toyotomi Hideyori|nl|Toyotomi Hideyori|no|Toyotomi Hideyori|pl|Hideyori Toyotomi|pt|Toyotomi Hideyori|ru|Тоётоми Хидэёри|sk|Hidejori Tojotomi|sr|Тојотоми Хидејори|th|โทโยโตมิ ฮิเดโยริ|tr|Toyotomi Hideyori|uk|Тойотомі Хідейорі|vi|Toyotomi Hideyori|zh|豐臣秀賴|qid=Q313641}} in {{ill|Keichō|Q1328185|qid=Q1328185}} 7th year ({{ill|1602|Q6727|qid=Q6727}}). An illustration from 2012 ({{ill|1656|Q6982|qid=Q6982}}) depicts the precincts and temple tower at the time of Hideyori's reconstruction. Going down from there, the current main shrine was built in {{ill|Bunsei|Q1327119|qid=Q1327119}}9 ({{ill|1826|Q7004|qid=Q7004}}) of the Edo period.

In addition, there were six {{ill|Jingū-ji|Q1074971|qid=Q1074971}} temples: Jingoji, Genkoan, Hiraokaji, Horenan, Raigoji, and Shindoji.{{Sfn|Hiraoka Four shrines (Shikinaisha)|1979}}{{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine (Heibonsha)|1986}}{{Sfn|Ichinomiya system in medieval countries|2000|pp=48-49}}. Jingo-ji Temple and Hiraoka-ji Temple are said to date back to the Middle Ages {{Sfn|Ichinomiya system in medieval countries|2000|pp=48-49}}.

=== Precincts ===
[[File:Hiraoka-jinja, honden-1.jpg|thumb|220px|right|{{center|Main shrine/transparent wall}}]]
[[File:Hiraoka-jinja haiden2.jpg|thumb|220px|right|{{center|Shrine}}]]
* Main shrine - Consists of 4 buildings. In the shrine precinct surrounded by the central gate and transparent wall, the second hall (Hime no Mikoto), first hall (Amagoyane no Mikoto), fourth hall (Takemikazuchi no Mikoto), and third hall (Ketsunushi no Mikoto) are lined up in a line from south to north in the north-south direction, directly facing the approach. The style of each hall is Hiraoka-zukuri, and the roof is {{ill|cypress bark roof|Q90373477|qid=Q90373477}}, and especially the first and second halls have a lot of old materials left. It looks similar to the main hall of Kasuga Taisha Shrine, but in the case of the main hall, the four buildings are independent. Although it does not maintain the traditions of ancient times, it is said to be a building that clearly shows the characteristics of the late to late Edo period with its tomata, rainbow beams, and wooden nose. </ref>{{Sfn|Higashiosaka City Designated Cultural Properties Revised Edition|2012}}. In addition, the shrine was constructed from the Heisei period to the Reiwa period, and restoration work was carried out to make it look like the shrine building from the late Edo period, which is confirmed in existing historical materials, so it has a unique form of the shrine building, which is Kasuga Shirenmaioka-zukuri, which is different from Kasuga-zukuri.
** First Hall (Tangible Cultural Property designated by Higashiosaka City) - Rebuilt in {{ill|Bunsei|Q1327119|qid=Q1327119}}9 ({{ill|1826|Q7004|qid=Q7004}}).** Second Hall (Tangible Cultural Property designated by Higashiosaka City) - Rebuilt in 1826.
** Third Hall (Tangible Cultural Property designated by Higashiosaka City) - Rebuilt in 1826.
** Fourth Hall (Tangible Cultural Property designated by Higashiosaka City) - Rebuilt in 1826.
* Middle gate
* Worship Hall - Rebuilt in {{ill|1879|Q7783|qid=Q7783}} ({{ill|Meiji era|Q3125096|qid=Q3125096}}12). <ref name="Hiraoka Shrine Main Hall"/> was built according to the status of the former Kanpei Taisha Shrine. The roof is made of copper sheets (formerly cypress bark), and the plaque ``Hiraoka Shrine'' is written by {{ill|Sanjō Sanetomi|Q516646|qid=Q516646}}<ref name="Precincts"/>.
* Gokaden
* Keimeiden (shrine office)
* Gathering place
* Saikan - Built in {{ill|1936|Q18649|qid=Q18649}} ({{ill|Shōwa era|Q327567|qid=Q327567}}11) as a shrine office. It is currently used as a funeral hall. </ref>.* Hiraoka Bairin (designated by Higashiosaka City as a scenic spot {{ill|Place of Scenic Beauty|Q11414752|qid=Q11414752}}) - The place where the {{ill|Ōbaku|Q384728|qid=Q384728}} Jingoji Temple of Hiraoka Shrine was once located. {{ill|1873|Q7757|qid=Q7757}} (Meiji 6) After Jingo-ji Temple was abandoned, volunteers from Toyoura village planted plum trees and set up a viewing platform on the site. {{ill|Taishō era|Q329174|qid=Q329174}}In the first year, it was developed and expanded by Osaka businessmen and Daiki no Shokokai, and in the early Showa period, by the Shinen Hoshokai.{{Sfn|Designated Cultural Property of Higashiosaka City Revised Edition|2012}}
* Kozudake Main Shrine - The place that is said to be the founding place of our company ({{Coord|34|40|4.56|N|135|39|25.78|E|region:JP-27_type:landmark|name=Kozudake Main Shrine}}), located on the east mountain top of the current shrine grounds. It was once a forbidden area, but a stone monument was built in {{ill|1981|Q2437|qid=Q2437}} (1981), and a stone shrine was built in {{ill|1993|Q2065|qid=Q2065}} ({{ill|Heisei era|Q234510|qid=Q234510}}5), and it remains today<ref name="Precincts"/>.The Ichi-no-Torii ({{Coord|34|40|7.64|N|135|38|29.39|E|region:JP-27_type:landmark|name=Hiraoka Shrine Ichi-no-Torii}}) is built along {{ill|Higashi Kōya Kaidō|Q11528777|qid=Q11528777}} about 800 meters west of the approach from the Nino-Torii. group="note">By the way, the name of the place where the first torii gate was built is Torii Town. </ref>. Kozudake can be seen in the front and back, and the approach to the shrine is called ``Matsu no Baba.'' The nearby stone lantern was once built in the center of the torii gate, and is the oldest in Higashiosaka city with an inscription dating back to {{ill|Jōkyō|Q1146221|qid=Q1146221}}2 ({{ill|1685|Q7660|qid=Q7660}}). The Ichino Torii and Matsu no Baba are also depicted in the Kawachi-kuni Hosomizu of 1776|Q7703}} ({{ill|An'ei|Q1193910|qid=Q1193910|lt=Yasunaga}}5 ({{ill|1776|Q7703|qid=Q7703}})<ref>Hiraoka Shrine Ichino Torii Historic Site Explanation Board (Higashiosaka City Board of Education, installed in 1991). </ref>.

=== Setsusha ===
[[File:Hiraoka-jinja, Wakamiya-sha.jpg|thumb|220px|right|{{center|Wakamiyasha}}]]
There are two Setsusha shrines, one Setsusha and one Setsusha (both are shrines within the precincts) <ref name="Yoshisho"/>.

'''Setsusha'''
* Wakamiyasha
** Deity enshrined: {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|Q91088537|qid=Q91088537}}
** Annual festival: {{ill|December 17|Q2413|qid=Q2413}}
*: The enshrined deity, Amenoosikumone, is the {{ill|Mikogami|de|Mikokami|ja|御子神|zh|御子神|qid=Q352176}} of Amagoyane no Mikoto. It is also enshrined as a Wakamiya shrine at Kasuga Taisha Shrine, etc.<ref name="Masaaki Ueda 2015"/>. Although it does not appear in "{{ill|Kojiki|Q813031|qid=Q813031}}" or "{{ill|Nihon Shoki|Q813935|qid=Q813935}}," in "{{ill|Nakatomi no Yogoto|Q24877078|qid=Q24877078}}" there is a legend that says that he climbed to the top of the heavens and took the water for the imperial grandchild.<ref name="Masaaki Ueda 2015">{{ill|Masaaki Ueda|Q3297094|qid=Q3297094}} "New Research on Ancient Japan and East Asia" Fujiwara Shoten, 2015, pp. 108-114. </ref><ref name="Precinct"/>. There is a well called ``Izumoi'' in the back of the shrine building (one theory is the origin of the place name Izumoi-cho) <ref name="Precincts"/>.

'''Suesha'''
* Tenjin Jigisha
** Deity enshrined: {{ill|Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|Q11442793|qid=Q11442793}}
** Annual festival: {{ill|March 25|Q2454|qid=Q2454}}*: When organizing the shrines in {{ill|1872|Q7753|qid=Q7753}} (Meiji 5), 19 subsidiary shrines in the precincts <ref name="Precincts"/> (or 15 subsidiary shrines {{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine 4-za (Shikiuchi-sha) |1979}}) and more than 20 nearby shrines {{Sfn|Hiraoka-jinja 4-za (Shikiuchi-sha)|1979}} are enshrined together. Some of them have since been re-enshrined after canceling their joint enshrinement.

=== Special ritual ===
; {{ill|Kayu ura|Q11604655|qid=Q11604655}} Shinto ritual
: "Kayuura Shiji". {{ill|January 11|Q2247|qid=Q2247|lt=January 15th}}.
: {{ill|koshōgatsu|Q137803901|qid=Q137803901}} yearly fortune telling ritual. Nowadays, due to advances in printing technology, the ritual is held on January 15th and the results are announced afterwards. In the ritual, 5 square meters of rice and 3 square meters of red beans are boiled in a large pot, and a bundle of 53 fortune-telling bamboos is hung inside the pot, and the red bean porridge inside the bamboo is used to predict the year's bountiful harvest. In addition, 12 black oak fortune-telling trees (13 in leap years) are placed in the stove, and the weather is predicted by the degree of charring of the trees. The Shinto ritual is also described in "Kawachi Kanmeishoki" {{Sfn|Hiraoka Shrine (Heibonsha)|1986}}. Selected as an Osaka Prefecture {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Selected Intangible Folk Cultural Property}}{{Sfn|Designated Cultural Property of Higashiosaka City Revised Edition|2012}}.
; Shimenawakake ritual (comedy ritual)
: "Shimekake Shinji". {{ill|December 23|Q2676|qid=Q2676}}.
: A ritual that invites spring through laughter. It used to be held on {{ill|January 8|Q2234|qid=Q2234}} before the porridge divine ritual. During the ritual, a large shimenawa rope is strung around a shimenawa pillar at the bottom of the stone steps, and the priests and parishioners laugh loudly under the shimenawa pillar, praying for the arrival of spring. It has been designated as an intangible folk cultural property designated by Higashiosaka City {{Sfn|Higashiosaka City Designated Cultural Property Revised Edition|2012}}.

=== Cultural assets ===

=== Osaka Prefecture Selected Intangible Folk Cultural Properties ===
* Congee fortune-telling ritual at Hiraoka Shrine (attached: Hiraoka Shrine Congee Diary Volume 1) - Selected on August 4, 1978 {{Sfn|Designated Cultural Property of Higashiosaka City Revised Edition|2012}}<ref From the Higashiosaka City file in name="Cultural Properties">[http://www.pref.osaka.lg.jp/bunkazaihogo/bunkazai/hunai-siteiichiran.html Osaka Prefecture Designated Cultural Properties List] (Osaka Prefecture homepage). </ref>.

=== Cultural property designated by Higashiosaka City ===
*Tangible cultural property
** Main shrine 4 buildings (buildings)
**: Constructed in {{ill|Bunsei|Q1327119|qid=Q1327119}}9 ({{ill|1826|Q7004|qid=Q7004}}) during the Edo period. It was designated on March 25, 1974, and eight bronze hanging lanterns were additionally designated on May 11, 1995.
** Hiraoka Shrine copper imitation jewel (craft)
**: Created in the early Edo period, {{ill|Keichō|Q1328185|qid=Q1328185}}7 ({{ill|1602|Q6727|qid=Q6727}}). This is a wooden bridge imitation jewel donated by Toyotomi Hideyori. It measures 36.5 centimeters in height and has an inscription engraved on its body. Designated on March 25, 1974 {{Sfn|Designated Cultural Property of Higashiosaka City Revised Edition|2012}}<ref name="Cultural Property"/>.
** Hiraoka Shrine copper hanging lantern (craft)
**: Created in the early Edo period, Keicho 8 ({{ill|1603|Q6735|qid=Q6735}}). Donation by Hideyori Toyotomi. It is hexagonal and measures 48.5 centimeters in height, and inscriptions are engraved on four sides of the firebox's pillars. Designated on March 25, 1974 {{Sfn|Designated Cultural Property of Higashiosaka City Revised Edition|2012}}<ref name="Cultural Property"/>.
** Colored illustration of Hiraoka Shrine on silk (painting)**: Written by Kano Hachirobei in the 2nd year of {{ill|Meireki|Q1192766|qid=Q1192766}} ({{ill|1656|Q6982|qid=Q6982}}) during the Edo period. Height: 196.5 cm, Width: 88.5 cm. There is a description of the background of the painting at the bottom left of the screen, which says that it is a drawing depicting the precincts as they were before they fell into disrepair in the 2nd year of Meireki. Designated on March 25, 1974 {{Sfn|Designated Cultural Property of Higashiosaka City Revised Edition|2012}}<ref name="Cultural Property"/>.
* Intangible folk cultural assets
** Shimenawakake ritual at Hiraoka Shrine - Designated on March 25, 1974 {{Sfn|Designated Cultural Property of Higashiosaka City Revised Edition|2012}}<ref name="Cultural Property"/>.
* Scenic spots
** Hiraoka Bairin - Designated on March 25, 1974 {{Sfn|Higashiosaka City Designated Cultural Property Revised Edition|2012}}<ref name="Cultural Property"/>.

=== Others ===
The {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=juniper}} on the temple grounds was once designated as a natural monument by Osaka Prefecture in 1938 (Showa 13), but it was damaged by {{ill|Typhoon Nancy (1961)|Q1140009|qid=Q1140009}} in {{ill|1961|Q3696|qid=Q3696}} (Showa 36) and was cut down in the 1960s.<ref name="Precinct"/>.
